{"answer": "# Elevated-temperature and impact testing of aluminum alloys

**The governing distinction is between a service-life target, time actually spent in a test furnace, and the much shorter duration of an impact.** The best-documented supersonic-airframe program below specified a 60,000-hour service objective but published tensile results after exposures of *up to 30,000 hours*; its 177 °C upper end is not supported by that tensile report. Impact programs instead measured deformation and failure over specified strain rates or projectile speeds, then tested whether a calibrated model predicted *other* impact conditions. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000062)

## Long-duration thermal qualification

| Program or material | Documented conditions | Properties and selection result | Traceable source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Concorde skin: 2618A / RR58-derived CM001** | Mach 2.05 skin maximum **approximately 130 °C**; design life **7,000 flights/15,000 hours**. Creep deformation and fatigue resistance informed its safe-life design. The 15,000 hours is a *design life*, not an exposure duration established by the cited source. | CM001 was made by modifying RR58 composition and processing to meet Concorde creep, durability, strength and fracture requirements. NASA identifies **2618 as the US equivalent** of RR58/CM001; equivalent designations do not make all tempers and product forms interchangeable. | Hénaff *et al.*, *Creep and Creep-Fatigue Crack Growth in Aluminium Alloys*, DOI **10.5772/15153**; Edahl and Domack, **NASA/TP-2004-212988**. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010) |
| **Later supersonic-skin creep–fatigue research: 2650-T6** | A proposed **20,000-flight/60,000-hour** life near **130 °C** motivated damage-tolerance work. *Actual 2650 tests*, not Concorde 2618A tests, included prior exposure **30,000 hours at 100 or 130 °C** and **20,000 hours at 175 °C**, followed by hardness and tensile tests; creep/crack-growth experiments principally covered **100–175 °C**. | No significant loss of measured properties after those prior exposures was reported. Compact-tension specimens were used for creep, fatigue and creep–fatigue crack growth; the study distinguishes their mechanisms and hold-time effects from simple uncracked tensile strength. | Hénaff *et al.*, DOI **10.5772/15153**. (pqac-00000008) |
| **NASA–University of Virginia HSCT screening** | **60,000 hours** was a performance objective and **120,000 hours** a stated certification goal—not demonstrated furnace-test durations. The program considered ingot-metallurgy **2xxx and 6xxx** families; **2519-T87** was a 2xxx baseline and **6013-T6** a 6xxx reference for lower-wing/fuselage concepts. | Screening addressed elevated-temperature strength retention, creep resistance and damage tolerance. The early program record does **not** establish that either reference alloy passed a 60,000-hour exposure test. | Starke, **NASA CR-4517** (1993); the subsequently cited program report is **NASA/CR-97-206248** (1997). (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000014) |
| **NASA HSCT long-exposure tensile comparison** | Exposures at **200, 225 and 275 °F (93, 107 and 135 °C)**, for **up to 30,000 hours**; tensile tests at **−65 °F, room temperature, 200, 225 and 275 °F**. Actual candidates were **C415, C416, RX818 and ML377**; **CM001/2618-equivalent and 1143** were comparators. **C415/C416 were derived from 2519, not specimens designated 2519; 6013 was not in this test matrix.** | Measured yield strength, ultimate strength, elongation and modulus, including orientation effects and both room-temperature *post-exposure* and *hot* tests. C415, C416 and ML377 retained tensile strength within roughly **5% through 30,000 hours at 200–225 °F**; after exposure at **275 °F for 15,000 hours**, candidate tensile-strength losses reached **25%**. RX818 was dropped after **5,000 hours** because a companion study found inadequate fracture toughness despite its high strength. NASA identified **200–225 °F** as the candidates’ upper service-temperature range. | Edahl and Domack, *Effect of Thermal Exposure on the Tensile Properties of Aluminum Alloys for Elevated Temperature Service*, **NASA/TP-2004-212988** (2004). Companion creep paper: Taminger *et al.*, “Evaluation of Creep Behavior of Emerging Aluminum Alloys for Supersonic Aircraft Applications,” *Proceedings of the 6th International Conference on Aluminum Alloys* (1998), pp. 1361–1366; the tensile report **does not itself supply creep-rupture allowables**. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014) |

**Temperature correction.** The documented long-exposure tensile campaign reached **135 °C**, not **177 °C**. A separate NASA hypersonic-structures discussion describes protecting a conventional aluminum airframe below **350 °F/177 °C**; that is a *structural temperature limit for a thermal-protection concept*, not evidence that the HSCT C415/C416 coupons were soaked at 177 °C for 60,000 hours. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000027)

**MMPDS.** MMPDS is the appropriate source to check alloy-, temper-, form-, thickness- and direction-specific design properties and elevated-temperature effects before establishing an allowable. Its definitions distinguish design yield and ultimate stresses and statistical A-/B-basis properties. The MMPDS material retrievable here did **not** provide a verified numerical prolonged-exposure curve for the particular alloy/temper combinations; consequently, neither a specific MMPDS exposure time nor an allowable is asserted. A short-duration hot tensile value must not be substituted for strength *after* long exposure or for creep performance. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013)

## Engine-adjacent, high-speed and additively manufactured applications

* **Nacelles, pylons, inlets and APUs:** These labels alone do not specify the metal temperature. A documented engine application is the **cast-2219 fan case**; it is **not** evidence for a 2219 compressor *wheel*. An industry materials survey instead identifies Inconel 718 in a nacelle area at temperatures up to **650 °C** and titanium in compressor structures, illustrating why the hot zone cannot automatically be assigned an aluminum allowable. The retrieved sources give no component-specific NASA/FAA/AFRL aluminum heat-soak matrix for a particular pylon, inlet or APU, so their service temperatures and exposure hours cannot responsibly be generalized. Boyer *et al.*, DOI **10.1557/mrs.2015.278**. (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035)
* **Compressor wheels and impellers:** A published **2618-versus-titanium impeller study at 50,000 rpm** is a *structural/CFD calculation*, not a reported hot creep-qualification campaign; DOI **10.3390/engproc2023059221**. Industry-associated turbocharger-wheel work used overspeed spin tests, surface metrology, fatigue specimens and fracture origins to investigate machining marks, but its reported result does not establish an elevated-temperature qualification of 2618 or 2219 wheels. Do not transfer fan-*case* data to rotating impellers. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000035)
* **Missiles and hypersonic vehicles:** NASA’s explicitly documented route for an aluminum hypersonic airframe is a **thermal-protection system keeping the conventional structure at or below 350 °F (177 °C)**; other routes are active cooling or a higher-temperature *non-aluminum* hot structure. The hypersonic exterior and an insulated aluminum substrate therefore do not share a test temperature. Tenney, Lisagor and Dixon, *Journal of Aircraft* (1989), DOI **10.2514/3.45868**. The sources examined do not establish an alloy-specific missile-aluminum exposure schedule. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000048)
* **Printed high-temperature aluminum:** An Oak Ridge-associated study of LPBF **Al–10Ce–8Mn** used hot tensile testing over **150–400 °C**, with a **30-minute equilibration**, and separately tested material pre-exposed **200 hours at 400 °C**; approximately **10⁻⁴ s⁻¹** was its initial tensile strain rate. It measured tensile behavior, hardness and microstructure rather than aircraft-component certification. Plotkowski *et al.*, *Acta Materialia* (2020), DOI **10.1016/j.actamat.2020.07.014**. LPBF **AlSi10Mg**, stress-relieved **2 hours at 350 °C**, was tensile-tested at room temperature, **125, 250 and 450 °C**: 0°-build ultimate strengths were **280.2, 162.8 and 34.4 MPa** at room temperature, 250 and 450 °C, respectively—evidence of why a printed bracket near an engine needs a measured *part-metal* temperature. Lehmhus *et al.*, DOI **10.3390/ma15207386**. (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000046)
* **Prototype versus qualification:** An **AlSi10Mg aircraft-engine cooling heat-exchanger prototype** was designed, printed and described for engine testing; the available thesis does **not** establish a certified high-temperature alloy allowable. Separately, a **DOE/ORNL–industry automotive-piston materials project** tested LPBF **Al–9Ce–4Ni–0.5Mn–1Zr** coupons after **350 °C/8 hours** heat treatment. Its tensile tests ran from room temperature through **350 °C at 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹**; fully reversed **50-Hz** fatigue tests at **150, 250 and 350 °C** used **10⁷ cycles** as runout, yielding respective fatigue strengths of **115, 100 and 60 MPa**. This is valuable engine-adjacent aluminum evidence, **not a NASA/FAA aerospace-part qualification**. Perrone (2019), *Prototype Development of an Innovative Heat Exchanger for an Aircraft Engine Cooling System Made by Additive Manufacturing*; Plotkowski, Rakhmonov and Ferlet, DOE report DOI **10.2172/2573209**. (pqac-00000052, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045)

## Crash, bird-strike and fan-containment testing

| Driver and documented test | Rate, impact condition and properties measured | Why it mattered; source |
|---|---|---|
| **Automotive crash-forming/body-sheet material** | Tensile split-Hopkinson tests on **AA5754 and AA5182** at **600, 1,100 and 1,500 s⁻¹**, compared with **3.3 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹** quasistatic tests; room- and elevated-temperature experiments measured stress–strain response and failure elongation. The paper describes an approximately **500 s⁻¹ nominal crash rate**, with higher local folding rates. | Flow-stress rate sensitivity was modest, but failure elongation increased markedly; fitted Johnson–Cook behavior therefore needs *ductility/failure* data as well as yield stress. Smerd *et al.*, *International Journal of Impact Engineering* (2005), DOI **10.1016/j.ijimpeng.2005.04.013**. These are sheet-alloy tests motivated by crashworthiness, not proof that the specimens were complete crash boxes. (pqac-00000065) |
| **FAA engine-fragment shielding/fan-containment model check** | **2024-T3** plates of **0.0625, 0.125 and 0.25 in.** were fired on with a **0.5-in. steel sphere**. Outcomes were ballistic limit, residual speed and *petaling versus plugging*. A Johnson–Cook model calibrated to **0.125 in.** overpredicted the thin plate’s ballistic limit and underpredicted the thick plate’s. | FAA pursued stress-state-, temperature- and rate-dependent **tabulated MAT_224** rather than treating one fitted Johnson–Cook failure parameter set as universally predictive. Cordasco, Emmerling and Du Bois, *11th European LS-DYNA Conference* (2017); related FAA report **DOT/FAA/AR-08/36**. (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062, pqac-00000064) |
| **FAA coupon calibration for 2024-T351** | One **0.5-in.-thick plate** supplied multiaxial deformation/fracture specimens spanning about **10⁻⁴–11,000 s⁻¹** and **50–450 °C** in the FAA program account. An independently published 2024-T351 study covered **10⁻⁴–10⁴ s⁻¹** and **−50 to 450 °C**, with tension, compression and shear. | Measured plastic flow, fracture strain, orientation dependence and stress-state dependence; rates alone were insufficient because the 2024 study found little plastic-flow rate effect up to roughly **5,000 s⁻¹** and noncoincident tension/compression/shear curves. Sources: **DOT/FAA/TC-13/25, Parts 1–3**; Seidt and Gilat, DOI **10.1016/j.ijsolstr.2013.02.006**. The two quoted temperature ranges come from *different accounts* and should not be conflated. (pqac-00000063, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000066) |
| **NASA Glenn/FAA ballistic validation** | NASA **NASA/TM-2012-217625** tested Al-2024 small panels at **0.125, 0.25 and 0.5 in.** with a **0.5-in. cylindrical projectile**, targeting penetration speeds around **600–900 ft/s (180–275 m/s)**; larger panels were also struck obliquely. Recorded impact/residual velocities, penetration, backside strain and displacement using high-speed imaging and digital-image correlation. Later oblique Al-2024 experiments covered **0°, 30° and 45°** panel tilt. | Plate-level measurements tested transfer of coupon-calibrated failure laws to actual penetration geometries. Pereira *et al.*, **NASA/TM-2012-217625**, journal DOI **10.1061/(ASCE)AS.1943-5525.0000356**; Ruggeri *et al.*, **NASA/TM-2015-218484 / DOT/FAA/TC-15/7**. **Projectile speed is not specimen strain rate**; neither memorandum establishes bird-strike resistance of an aluminum fan blade. (pqac-00000069, pqac-00000070, pqac-00000067, pqac-00000071) |

**Regulatory and bird-strike boundary:** FAA identifies fan-blade-off containment under **14 CFR 33.94** as requiring an *engine test*; analysis is supplementary and needs validation. Bird ingestion/strike is a related but different load case: an illustrative *simulation* compares **2024-T3 and 7075-T6** plates under soft impacts of **117 and 147 m/s**, using assigned Johnson–Cook parameters. Those speeds are simulation inputs, **not measured coupon strain rates or FAA material qualification tests**. In particular, a Johnson–Cook fit should report the tested alloy/temper, temperature, plastic strain and rate range, failure stress states, and independent plate/component validation—not merely a parameter list. FAA conference paper above; Aslam *et al.*, DOI **10.1088/1742-6596/1707/1/012008**. (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000059)

**Evidence limit:** The documents establish strong examples of how programs *selected and evaluated* aluminum, and of how impact data improved predictive models. They do not jointly document a completed 60,000-hour HSCT soak, a verified MMPDS thermal-exposure allowable, or alloy-specific certified tests for every proposed nacelle, APU, missile, printed bracket, bird-strike component or 2219 impeller. Reporting those as completed qualification campaigns would exceed the available evidence. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000061)"}

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the NASA report as NASA/TP-2004-212988, titled “Effect of Thermal Exposure on the Tensile Properties of Aluminum Alloys for Elevated Temperature Service,” by Robert A. Edahl, Jr. and Marcia S. Domack. It evaluates candidate alloys C415, C416, RX818, and ML377, with comparison alloys CM001 and 1143. Thermal exposures were conducted at 200°F, 225°F, and 275°F for up to 30,000 hours. Tensile testing covered as-received and thermally exposed material at −65°F, room temperature, 200°F, 225°F, and 275°F, allowing room-temperature and elevated-temperature tensile properties to be compared. After 30,000 hours at 200°F and 225°F, C415, C416, and ML377 had only minor decreases in yield strength, tensile strength, and elongation; after 15,000 hours at 275°F, tensile-strength reductions reached 25%. The Concorde alloy is identified as CM001, whose U.S. Aluminum Association equivalent is 2618; the excerpt states that CM001 processing was tailored to optimize creep properties. It does not provide an NTRS identifier beyond the report number, data for alloys 2519 or 6013, specific “2618A” exposure results, or MMPDS interpretation. Those points require another source or later pages of the report.

contexts.context: The excerpt is from Edahl and Domack, “Effect of thermal exposure on the tensile properties of aluminum alloys for elevated temperature service,” pages 8–14, and provides experimental procedures rather than the requested report-identification or complete alloy-results information. It states that candidate and baseline alloys were exposed isothermally for up to 30,000 hours at 200, 225, and 275°F; machined specimens covered exposures up to 1,000 hours, while larger sheet sections were used for 3,000–30,000 hours. RX818 was discontinued after 5,000 hours because of poor fracture toughness. Tensile specimens were tested longitudinally, transversely, and at 45° according to ASTM E8, using a constant stroke rate of 0.0625 in/min. As-received materials were tested at room temperature, 200, 225, 275°F, and −65°F; post-exposure testing was primarily at room temperature, with some tests at exposure or cryogenic temperatures. Yield strength was measured using the 0.2% offset method, and modulus generally over 0.1–0.5% strain. The excerpt includes C415 and C416 figure references and discusses CM001 and 1143, including Concorde-related creep and strength goals. It does not provide an NTRS identifier/report number, data for alloys 2519 or 6013, detailed C415/C416 results, 2618A exposure/creep results, or an MMPDS interpretation.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents Concorde’s 2618A fuselage skin at a Mach 2.05 maximum temperature of 130°C, designed for 7,000 flights/15,000 h using creep deformation and fatigue resistance; a later supersonic design required 20,000 flights/60,000 h at approximately 130°C and damage-tolerance crack-growth modeling. contexts.question: How have aerospace and automotive programs documented elevated-temperature and strain-rate testing to select and qualify aluminum alloys? Examples: Concorde's 2618A (RR58 / AU2GN) skin and its long-time creep and thermal-exposure testing at about 100-130 C; the NASA High-Speed Research (HSCT) program's evaluation of 2xxx and 6xxx alloys (for example C415, C416, 2519, 6013) for 60,000 h at about 107-177 C; MMPDS thermal-exposure data; aluminum in engine nacelles, pylons, inlets and auxiliary power units; 2618 and 2219 in compressor wheels and impellers; aluminum on missiles and hypersonic vehicles; and additively manufactured high-temperature aluminum parts (heat exchangers, brackets near engines). Also crash and impact testing of aluminum (automotive crash boxes, bird strike, fan-blade containment) that drove high-strain-rate testing and Johnson-Cook calibration. For each, give the temperatures, exposure times or strain rates used, the properties measured, and NASA, FAA or AFRL technical reports or conference papers with citations, DOIs or NTRS numbers.

contexts.context: The HSCT airframe study tested C415, C416, RX818, and ML377 (versus Concorde CM001 and 1143) at −65°F, room temperature, 200°F, 225°F, and 275°F after exposures up to 30,000 h. Tensile yield/ultimate strength, elongation, and stress–strain behavior were measured. Strength remained within 5% after 10,000 h at 200–225°F and up to 30,000 h for ML377/C415/C416, but fell 5–25% after 275°F exposure; 200–225°F was identified as the service limit. Sources: NASA CR-97-206248 and Lockheed report LG97ER0037.
contexts.question: How have aerospace and automotive programs documented elevated-temperature and strain-rate testing to select and qualify aluminum alloys? Examples: Concorde's 2618A (RR58 / AU2GN) skin and its long-time creep and thermal-exposure testing at about 100-130 C; the NASA High-Speed Research (HSCT) program's evaluation of 2xxx and 6xxx alloys (for example C415, C416, 2519, 6013) for 60,000 h at about 107-177 C; MMPDS thermal-exposure data; aluminum in engine nacelles, pylons, inlets and auxiliary power units; 2618 and 2219 in compressor wheels and impellers; aluminum on missiles and hypersonic vehicles; and additively manufactured high-temperature aluminum parts (heat exchangers, brackets near engines). Also crash and impact testing of aluminum (automotive crash boxes, bird strike, fan-blade containment) that drove high-strain-rate testing and Johnson-Cook calibration. For each, give the temperatures, exposure times or strain rates used, the properties measured, and NASA, FAA or AFRL technical reports or conference papers with citations, DOIs or NTRS numbers.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns hydrogen-environment embrittlement, not aerospace elevated-temperature or strain-rate qualification. A 50-year database primarily reports tests at room temperature (24°C) and hydrogen pressures of 5–10 ksi (34.5–69 MPa). HEE indices are ratios of hydrogen-to-air/helium properties, including notched tensile strength, elongation, and reduction in area. Aluminum examples include 1100-T0, 2011/2024, 5086, 6061-T6, 6063, 7039, and 7075-T73, generally rated “negligible,” with indices near unity. The excerpt warns these data “should not be used to estimate the HEE effects at high temperature” or replace fracture analysis.

snippets: Starke, E. A., Jr.: NASA - UVA Light Aerospace Alloy and Structure Technology Program Supplement: Aluminum - Based Materials for High Speed Aircraft. NASA CR-97-206248, December 1997.

Tensile properties were evaluated for material in the as-received (T8 or T6) condition at -65˚F, room temperature, 200˚F, 225˚F and 275˚F and after thermal exposure at 200˚F, 225˚F and 275˚F for times up to 30,000 hours.

Tensile strengths of the candidate and baseline alloys were stable within 5% after 10,000 hours exposure at 200˚F and 225˚F, and remained stable for alloys ML377, C415, and C416 with continued exposure for up to 30,000 hours.
After exposure at 275˚F, however, reductions in tensile strength were from 5% to 25% for the four candidate alloys when compared with results for as-received material.

The change in microstructure due to precipitate coarsening that occurred after 10,000 hours exposure at 275˚F, and the resulting reduction in yield strength, indicated that 200˚F-225˚F is the upper service temperature range for the candidate alloys.

At 275°F, tensile-strength reductions reached up to 25% after 15,000 hours for those alloys. The excerpt does not provide information on alloys 6013 or 2519, testing at 350°F, creep, fatigue, fracture toughness, certification to 120,000 hours, or detailed numerical property tables. Therefore, any 60,000-hour value or 120,000-hour certification target must be distinguished from the actual exposure durations documented here; this excerpt documents testing only through 30,000 hours.

contexts.context: The excerpt is only indirectly relevant to the requested investigation. It documents a 2019 University of Huddersfield doctoral thesis by Md Shams E Tabriz, conducted with BorgWarner Turbo Systems, on machining marks, stress distribution, and fatigue durability in turbocharger compressor wheels. The work compares nominal and measured (“as machined”) wheel geometry using CT scanning, optical surface measurement, CAD reconstruction, and finite-element analysis. Testing two wheel types at 10% above the design speed limit found fatigue failure initiating at machining marks in approximately 83% of cases. Reverse-engineered geometries produced maximum principal stresses 20–36% higher than nominal CAD models. The thesis also examined machining cusps, tool size, cusp depth, tool direction, surface curvature, and machining parameters, and developed regression models for stress-concentration effects. Optimising cusp specifications for five Type B compressor wheels increased fatigue life by 34%. However, these pages provide no alloy designation such as aluminum 2219 or 2618, no compressor-wheel test temperatures, no actual operating metal temperatures, and no evidence concerning cast fan cases, nacelles, pylons, inlets, APUs, or hypersonic insulated/protected aluminum structures. contexts.context: Tenney, Lisagor, and Dixon’s 1989 *Journal of Aircraft* paper surveys NASA Langley hypersonic-vehicle materials and structures research, including NASP. It states shuttle-style thermal protection permits a conventional aluminum airframe only to about **350°F (177°C)**, while reentry environments may reach **3000°F**; alternatives are active cooling or hot structures using high-temperature materials. The paper emphasizes that composites and ceramic-matrix composites require extensive “materials development, process development, scaleup, fabrication technologies, property characterization, and proof-of-concept studies.” Presented as **AIAA Paper 88-2.3.1** at ICAS (Jerusalem, 1988); published November 1989, pp. 953954 onward.
contexts.question: How have aerospace and automotive programs documented elevated-temperature and strain-rate testing to select and qualify aluminum alloys? Examples: Concorde's 2618A (RR58 / AU2GN) skin and its long-time creep and thermal-exposure testing at about 100-130 C; the NASA High-Speed Research (HSCT) program's evaluation of 2xxx and 6xxx alloys (for example C415, C416, 2519, 6013) for 60,000 h at about 107-177 C; MMPDS thermal-exposure data; aluminum in engine nacelles, pylons, inlets and auxiliary power units; 2618 and 2219 in compressor wheels and impellers; aluminum on missiles and hypersonic vehicles; and additively manufactured high-temperature aluminum parts (heat exchangers, brackets near engines). Also crash and impact testing of aluminum (automotive crash boxes, bird strike, fan-blade containment) that drove high-strain-rate testing and Johnson-Cook calibration. For each, give the temperatures, exposure times or strain rates used, the properties measured, and NASA, FAA or AFRL technical reports or conference papers with citations, DOIs or NTRS numbers.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns laser powder bed fused A205, an Al-Cu-Mg-Ag-TiB2 high-strength aluminum alloy, and compares as-fabricated, Standard T7, Commercial, and novel Rapid heat treatments. It provides useful thermal-mechanical test conditions but does not report the requested complete dataset of stress-relief or soak durations, numerical yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, ductility, corrosion measurements, or source DOI. Fatigue testing was conducted at room temperature under a fixed 180 MPa load. The Rapid heat treatment produced approximately 189% and 125% higher fatigue life than the Standard T7 and Commercial treatments, respectively. Creep testing was performed at 180 °C and 200 MPa; Rapid HT showed the highest resistance, with creep life exceeding 24 hours and approximately 33% and 80% improvement over Standard T7 and Commercial HT. The Rapid HT used a single solution step, retained a fine grain size, and generated a high density of fine precipitates. It reduced total processing time by approximately 67% relative to Standard T7 and 25% relative to Commercial HT. The excerpt identifies the study as relevant to A205 additive manufacturing, but it does not establish that the tests were specifically performed on a heat-exchanger component. References include related A205 fatigue and creep publications, but no DOI is given here.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides data for the actually additively manufactured Al-9Ce-4Ni-0.5Mn-1Zr alloy, identified in the results as AlCeNiMnZr (also called DuAlumin-3D), produced by laser powder bed fusion and heat treated. The source is Plotkowski, Rakhmonov, and Ferlet, 2025, DOI 10.2172/2573209.

contexts.context: This excerpt identifies the Plotkowski et al. ORNL study as a laser powder bed fusion investigation of an Al–10Ce–8Mn alloy, with the measured as-fabricated composition reported as approximately 10 wt% Ce and 7.68–7.71 wt% Mn, balance Al. contexts.context: The excerpt reports laser-powder-bed-fused Al-9Ce-4Ni-0.5Mn-1Zr (AlCeNiMnZr) tested against 2618, A201, and AlSi10Mg. Thermal conductivity, expansion (to 350°C), tensile strength/elongation, and high-cycle fatigue were measured. AlCeNiMnZr had 81 GPa modulus and 137 W/mK conductivity; above ~250–300°C it surpassed 2618/A201 in strength. Fatigue tests stopped at 10 million cycles: strength was 115 MPa at 150°C, 100 MPa at 250°C, and 60 MPa at 350°C, still exceeding 2618 at 350°C. Pore-initiated fatigue cracking was documented fractographically.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides useful information for the Seidt–Gilat (2013) portion of the question, but it does not identify FAA Cordasco/Emmerling 2017 reports, FAA report identifiers, or provide the requested exact Lesuer DOT/FAA/AR-00/25 test matrix. Seidt and Gilat studied 12.7 mm 2024-T351 aluminum plate in uniaxial tension, compression, and pure shear over approximately 10^-4 to 10^4 s^-1 and temperatures from -50 to 450 °C. They report negligible strain-rate effects up to about 5000 s^-1, with rate sensitivity appearing in compression above that level. Increasing temperature reduced stress, and strain hardening was absent at 300 and 450 °C. The study found that effective stress–equivalent strain curves from tension, compression, and shear did not coincide, challenging J2 flow-theory-based plasticity models. It also found anisotropic plastic behavior depending on specimen orientation relative to the plate rolling direction. The data were used to calibrate and assess the Johnson–Cook (1983) model and Barlat et al. (1991) anisotropic yield function. The introduction cites prior work indicating minor or negligible rate sensitivity in 2024-T3/T351 over lower rate ranges, but the excerpt does not contain automotive Smerd (2005) results or detailed Johnson–Cook parameter limitations.

It also does not discuss the automotive alloy experiments of Smerd (2005), the rate and temperature ranges reported by Seidt and Gilat (2013), or their specific criticisms and limitations of the Johnson–Cook model. The relevant background is that Johnson–Cook plasticity represents stress as dependent on plastic strain, strain rate, and homologous temperature, while its damage formulation makes fracture strain dependent on stress triaxiality, strain rate, and temperature. contexts.context: The excerpt describes FAA research on simulating failure of aerospace aluminum and developing predictive LS-DYNA material models. Initial tests characterized aerospace metallic alloys and ballistic limits, using 2024-T3 aluminum plates with thicknesses of 0.0625, 0.125, and 0.25 inches and a 0.5-inch spherical steel projectile. The observed failure transitioned from dishing and petaling in thin plates toward plugging as thickness increased. Johnson-Cook MAT_15 simulations could reproduce the thickness for which parameters were calibrated, but overpredicted the ballistic limit for the thinnest plate and underpredicted it for the thickest; therefore, one parameter set could not represent all thicknesses and failure modes. The excerpt states that changes in thickness, velocity, or projectile shape may require retuning. FAA subsequently pursued MAT_224, MAT_224_GYS, and MAT_264, using tabulated plastic failure strain as a function of stress state, with temperature and strain-rate dependence. MAT_224 additionally represents the full three-dimensional stress state through stress triaxiality and the Lode parameter, enabling petaling, plugging, and intermediate transitions. contexts.context: The excerpt provides relevant ballistic-impact data for Al 2024-T3, but it does not identify FAA or NASA Glenn Research Center (GRC) report numbers, nor does it mention Pereira (2014), Ruggeri (2015), titanium plates, or their DOIs. The study uses LS-DYNA finite-element analysis with a Johnson–Cook viscoplastic model and a rigid steel cylindrical projectile. It examines projectile velocities from 50 to 900 m/s and Al 2024-T3 target thicknesses from 3.18 to 6.35 mm. The analytical comparison uses residual projectile velocities, while the principal response quantities include ballistic limit velocity and energy absorption. The reported ballistic-limit velocities rise from 97 m/s for the thinnest target to 183 m/s for the 6.35 mm target; the abstract identifies 183 m/s and 6.35 mm as producing the highest energy absorption behavior. Failure morphology depends on thickness: thinner targets show two-petal petalling, whereas 4.00 and 6.35 mm targets exhibit complete plugging without petals. The introduction also notes that impact produces plastic deformation, strain-rate and temperature effects, heating, friction, and mechanisms including spalling, petalling, and plugging. Thus, the excerpt can support general Al 2024 ballistic-impact parameters, but not the requested FAA/NASA documentation or specific Pereira/Ruggeri references.

Question: How have aerospace and automotive programs documented elevated-temperature and strain-rate testing to select and qualify aluminum alloys? Examples: Concorde's 2618A (RR58 / AU2GN) skin and its long-time creep and thermal-exposure testing at about 100-130 C; the NASA High-Speed Research (HSCT) program's evaluation of 2xxx and 6xxx alloys (for example C415, C416, 2519, 6013) for 60,000 h at about 107-177 C; MMPDS thermal-exposure data; aluminum in engine nacelles, pylons, inlets and auxiliary power units; 2618 and 2219 in compressor wheels and impellers; aluminum on missiles and hypersonic vehicles; and additively manufactured high-temperature aluminum parts (heat exchangers, brackets near engines). Also crash and impact testing of aluminum (automotive crash boxes, bird strike, fan-blade containment) that drove high-strain-rate testing and Johnson-Cook calibration. For each, give the temperatures, exposure times or strain rates used, the properties measured, and NASA, FAA or AFRL technical reports or conference papers with citations, DOIs or NTRS numbers.

# Elevated-temperature and impact testing of aluminum alloys

**The governing distinction is between a service-life target, time actually spent in a test furnace, and the much shorter duration of an impact.** The best-documented supersonic-airframe program below specified a 60,000-hour service objective but published tensile results after exposures of *up to 30,000 hours*; its 177 °C upper end is not supported by that tensile report. Impact programs instead measured deformation and failure over specified strain rates or projectile speeds, then tested whether a calibrated model predicted *other* impact conditions. (jr2004effectofthermal pages 1-5, jr1993nasauvalightaerospace pages 226-226, cordasco2017astatusreview pages 2-5)

## Long-duration thermal qualification

| Program or material | Documented conditions | Properties and selection result | Traceable source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Concorde skin: 2618A / RR58-derived CM001** | Mach 2.05 skin maximum **approximately 130 °C**; design life **7,000 flights/15,000 hours**. Creep deformation and fatigue resistance informed its safe-life design. The 15,000 hours is a *design life*, not an exposure duration established by the cited source. | CM001 was made by modifying RR58 composition and processing to meet Concorde creep, durability, strength and fracture requirements. NASA identifies **2618 as the US equivalent** of RR58/CM001; equivalent designations do not make all tempers and product forms interchangeable. | Hénaff *et al.*, *Creep and Creep-Fatigue Crack Growth in Aluminium Alloys*, DOI **10.5772/15153**; Edahl and Domack, **NASA/TP-2004-212988**. (hnaff2011creepandcreepfatigue pages 1-3, jr2004effectofthermal pages 1-5, jr2004effectofthermal pages 5-8) |
| **Later supersonic-skin creep–fatigue research: 2650-T6** | A proposed **20,000-flight/60,000-hour** life near **130 °C** motivated damage-tolerance work. *Actual 2650 tests*, not Concorde 2618A tests, included prior exposure **30,000 hours at 100 or 130 °C** and **20,000 hours at 175 °C**, followed by hardness and tensile tests; creep/crack-growth experiments principally covered **100–175 °C**. | No significant loss of measured properties after those prior exposures was reported. Compact-tension specimens were used for creep, fatigue and creep–fatigue crack growth; the study distinguishes their mechanisms and hold-time effects from simple uncracked tensile strength. | Hénaff *et al.*, DOI **10.5772/15153**. (hnaff2011creepandcreepfatigue pages 1-3) |
| **NASA–University of Virginia HSCT screening** | **60,000 hours** was a performance objective and **120,000 hours** a stated certification goal—not demonstrated furnace-test durations. The program considered ingot-metallurgy **2xxx and 6xxx** families; **2519-T87** was a 2xxx baseline and **6013-T6** a 6xxx reference for lower-wing/fuselage concepts. | Screening addressed elevated-temperature strength retention, creep resistance and damage tolerance. The early program record does **not** establish that either reference alloy passed a 60,000-hour exposure test. | Starke, **NASA CR-4517** (1993); the subsequently cited program report is **NASA/CR-97-206248** (1997). (jr1993nasauvalightaerospace pages 226-226, jr1993nasauvalightaerospace pages 5-9, jr1993nasauvalightaerospace pages 14-18, jr2004effectofthermal pages 28-32) |
| **NASA HSCT long-exposure tensile comparison** | Exposures at **200, 225 and 275 °F (93, 107 and 135 °C)**, for **up to 30,000 hours**; tensile tests at **−65 °F, room temperature, 200, 225 and 275 °F**. Actual candidates were **C415, C416, RX818 and ML377**; **CM001/2618-equivalent and 1143** were comparators. **C415/C416 were derived from 2519, not specimens designated 2519; 6013 was not in this test matrix.** | Measured yield strength, ultimate strength, elongation and modulus, including orientation effects and both room-temperature *post-exposure* and *hot* tests. C415, C416 and ML377 retained tensile strength within roughly **5% through 30,000 hours at 200–225 °F**; after exposure at **275 °F for 15,000 hours**, candidate tensile-strength losses reached **25%**. RX818 was dropped after **5,000 hours** because a companion study found inadequate fracture toughness despite its high strength. NASA identified **200–225 °F** as the candidates’ upper service-temperature range. | Edahl and Domack, *Effect of Thermal Exposure on the Tensile Properties of Aluminum Alloys for Elevated Temperature Service*, **NASA/TP-2004-212988** (2004). Companion creep paper: Taminger *et al.*, “Evaluation of Creep Behavior of Emerging Aluminum Alloys for Supersonic Aircraft Applications,” *Proceedings of the 6th International Conference on Aluminum Alloys* (1998), pp. 1361–1366; the tensile report **does not itself supply creep-rupture allowables**. (jr2004effectofthermal pages 1-5, jr2004effectofthermal pages 5-8, jr2004effectofthermal pages 25-28, jr2004effectofthermal pages 28-32) |

**Temperature correction.** The documented long-exposure tensile campaign reached **135 °C**, not **177 °C**. A separate NASA hypersonic-structures discussion describes protecting a conventional aluminum airframe below **350 °F/177 °C**; that is a *structural temperature limit for a thermal-protection concept*, not evidence that the HSCT C415/C416 coupons were soaked at 177 °C for 60,000 hours. (jr2004effectofthermal pages 1-5, tenney1989materialsandstructures pages 1-2)

**MMPDS.** MMPDS is the appropriate source to check alloy-, temper-, form-, thickness- and direction-specific design properties and elevated-temperature effects before establishing an allowable. Its definitions distinguish design yield and ultimate stresses and statistical A-/B-basis properties. The MMPDS material retrievable here did **not** provide a verified numerical prolonged-exposure curve for the particular alloy/temper combinations; consequently, neither a specific MMPDS exposure time nor an allowable is asserted. A short-duration hot tensile value must not be substituted for strength *after* long exposure or for creep performance. (standard2003a.0glossary pages 1-4, jr2004effectofthermal pages 1-5, jr2004effectofthermal pages 25-28)

## Engine-adjacent, high-speed and additively manufactured applications

* **Nacelles, pylons, inlets and APUs:** These labels alone do not specify the metal temperature. A documented engine application is the **cast-2219 fan case**; it is **not** evidence for a 2219 compressor *wheel*. An industry materials survey instead identifies Inconel 718 in a nacelle area at temperatures up to **650 °C** and titanium in compressor structures, illustrating why the hot zone cannot automatically be assigned an aluminum allowable. The retrieved sources give no component-specific NASA/FAA/AFRL aluminum heat-soak matrix for a particular pylon, inlet or APU, so their service temperatures and exposure hours cannot responsibly be generalized. Boyer *et al.*, DOI **10.1557/mrs.2015.278**. (boyer2015materialsconsiderationsfor pages 7-8, boyer2015materialsconsiderationsfor pages 8-9)
* **Compressor wheels and impellers:** A published **2618-versus-titanium impeller study at 50,000 rpm** is a *structural/CFD calculation*, not a reported hot creep-qualification campaign; DOI **10.3390/engproc2023059221**. Industry-associated turbocharger-wheel work used overspeed spin tests, surface metrology, fatigue specimens and fracture origins to investigate machining marks, but its reported result does not establish an elevated-temperature qualification of 2618 or 2219 wheels. Do not transfer fan-*case* data to rotating impellers. (ravinath2024optimizingandanalyzing pages 1-2, tabriz2019theeffectof pages 1-10, boyer2015materialsconsiderationsfor pages 8-9)
* **Missiles and hypersonic vehicles:** NASA’s explicitly documented route for an aluminum hypersonic airframe is a **thermal-protection system keeping the conventional structure at or below 350 °F (177 °C)**; other routes are active cooling or a higher-temperature *non-aluminum* hot structure. The hypersonic exterior and an insulated aluminum substrate therefore do not share a test temperature. Tenney, Lisagor and Dixon, *Journal of Aircraft* (1989), DOI **10.2514/3.45868**. The sources examined do not establish an alloy-specific missile-aluminum exposure schedule. (tenney1989materialsandstructures pages 1-2, tenney1989materialsandstructures pages 5-6)
* **Printed high-temperature aluminum:** An Oak Ridge-associated study of LPBF **Al–10Ce–8Mn** used hot tensile testing over **150–400 °C**, with a **30-minute equilibration**, and separately tested material pre-exposed **200 hours at 400 °C**; approximately **10⁻⁴ s⁻¹** was its initial tensile strain rate. It measured tensile behavior, hardness and microstructure rather than aircraft-component certification. Plotkowski *et al.*, *Acta Materialia* (2020), DOI **10.1016/j.actamat.2020.07.014**. LPBF **AlSi10Mg**, stress-relieved **2 hours at 350 °C**, was tensile-tested at room temperature, **125, 250 and 450 °C**: 0°-build ultimate strengths were **280.2, 162.8 and 34.4 MPa** at room temperature, 250 and 450 °C, respectively—evidence of why a printed bracket near an engine needs a measured *part-metal* temperature. Lehmhus *et al.*, DOI **10.3390/ma15207386**. (plotkowski2020microstructureandproperties pages 2-3, plotkowski2020microstructureandproperties pages 3-4, lehmhus2022hightemperaturemechanicalproperties pages 1-2)
* **Prototype versus qualification:** An **AlSi10Mg aircraft-engine cooling heat-exchanger prototype** was designed, printed and described for engine testing; the available thesis does **not** establish a certified high-temperature alloy allowable. Separately, a **DOE/ORNL–industry automotive-piston materials project** tested LPBF **Al–9Ce–4Ni–0.5Mn–1Zr** coupons after **350 °C/8 hours** heat treatment. Its tensile tests ran from room temperature through **350 °C at 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹**; fully reversed **50-Hz** fatigue tests at **150, 250 and 350 °C** used **10⁷ cycles** as runout, yielding respective fatigue strengths of **115, 100 and 60 MPa**. This is valuable engine-adjacent aluminum evidence, **not a NASA/FAA aerospace-part qualification**. Perrone (2019), *Prototype Development of an Innovative Heat Exchanger for an Aircraft Engine Cooling System Made by Additive Manufacturing*; Plotkowski, Rakhmonov and Ferlet, DOE report DOI **10.2172/2573209**. (perrone2019prototypedevelopmentof pages 1-6, plotkowski2025additivelymanufacturinghightemperature pages 8-12, plotkowski2025additivelymanufacturinghightemperature pages 12-17)

## Crash, bird-strike and fan-containment testing

| Driver and documented test | Rate, impact condition and properties measured | Why it mattered; source |
|---|---|---|
| **Automotive crash-forming/body-sheet material** | Tensile split-Hopkinson tests on **AA5754 and AA5182** at **600, 1,100 and 1,500 s⁻¹**, compared with **3.3 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹** quasistatic tests; room- and elevated-temperature experiments measured stress–strain response and failure elongation. The paper describes an approximately **500 s⁻¹ nominal crash rate**, with higher local folding rates. | Flow-stress rate sensitivity was modest, but failure elongation increased markedly; fitted Johnson–Cook behavior therefore needs *ductility/failure* data as well as yield stress. Smerd *et al.*, *International Journal of Impact Engineering* (2005), DOI **10.1016/j.ijimpeng.2005.04.013**. These are sheet-alloy tests motivated by crashworthiness, not proof that the specimens were complete crash boxes. (smerd2005highstrainrate pages 1-3) |
| **FAA engine-fragment shielding/fan-containment model check** | **2024-T3** plates of **0.0625, 0.125 and 0.25 in.** were fired on with a **0.5-in. steel sphere**. Outcomes were ballistic limit, residual speed and *petaling versus plugging*. A Johnson–Cook model calibrated to **0.125 in.** overpredicted the thin plate’s ballistic limit and underpredicted the thick plate’s. | FAA pursued stress-state-, temperature- and rate-dependent **tabulated MAT_224** rather than treating one fitted Johnson–Cook failure parameter set as universally predictive. Cordasco, Emmerling and Du Bois, *11th European LS-DYNA Conference* (2017); related FAA report **DOT/FAA/AR-08/36**. (cordasco2017astatusreview pages 1-2, cordasco2017astatusreview pages 2-5, cordasco2017astatusreview pages 14-15) |
| **FAA coupon calibration for 2024-T351** | One **0.5-in.-thick plate** supplied multiaxial deformation/fracture specimens spanning about **10⁻⁴–11,000 s⁻¹** and **50–450 °C** in the FAA program account. An independently published 2024-T351 study covered **10⁻⁴–10⁴ s⁻¹** and **−50 to 450 °C**, with tension, compression and shear. | Measured plastic flow, fracture strain, orientation dependence and stress-state dependence; rates alone were insufficient because the 2024 study found little plastic-flow rate effect up to roughly **5,000 s⁻¹** and noncoincident tension/compression/shear curves. Sources: **DOT/FAA/TC-13/25, Parts 1–3**; Seidt and Gilat, DOI **10.1016/j.ijsolstr.2013.02.006**. The two quoted temperature ranges come from *different accounts* and should not be conflated. (cordasco2017astatusreview pages 5-8, cordasco2017astatusreview pages 14-15, seidt2013plasticdeformationof pages 1-2) |
| **NASA Glenn/FAA ballistic validation** | NASA **NASA/TM-2012-217625** tested Al-2024 small panels at **0.125, 0.25 and 0.5 in.** with a **0.5-in. cylindrical projectile**, targeting penetration speeds around **600–900 ft/s (180–275 m/s)**; larger panels were also struck obliquely. Recorded impact/residual velocities, penetration, backside strain and displacement using high-speed imaging and digital-image correlation. Later oblique Al-2024 experiments covered **0°, 30° and 45°** panel tilt. | Plate-level measurements tested transfer of coupon-calibrated failure laws to actual penetration geometries. Pereira *et al.*, **NASA/TM-2012-217625**, journal DOI **10.1061/(ASCE)AS.1943-5525.0000356**; Ruggeri *et al.*, **NASA/TM-2015-218484 / DOT/FAA/TC-15/7**. **Projectile speed is not specimen strain rate**; neither memorandum establishes bird-strike resistance of an aluminum fan blade. (pereira2014ballisticimpacttesting pages 5-8, pereira2014ballisticimpacttesting pages 8-11, ruggeri2015impactandpenetration pages 1-5, ruggeri2015impactandpenetration pages 7-9) |

**Regulatory and bird-strike boundary:** FAA identifies fan-blade-off containment under **14 CFR 33.94** as requiring an *engine test*; analysis is supplementary and needs validation. Bird ingestion/strike is a related but different load case: an illustrative *simulation* compares **2024-T3 and 7075-T6** plates under soft impacts of **117 and 147 m/s**, using assigned Johnson–Cook parameters. Those speeds are simulation inputs, **not measured coupon strain rates or FAA material qualification tests**. In particular, a Johnson–Cook fit should report the tested alloy/temper, temperature, plastic strain and rate range, failure stress states, and independent plate/component validation—not merely a parameter list. FAA conference paper above; Aslam *et al.*, DOI **10.1088/1742-6596/1707/1/012008**. (cordasco2017astatusreview pages 1-2, cordasco2017astatusreview pages 2-5, cordasco2017astatusreview pages 5-8)

**Evidence limit:** The documents establish strong examples of how programs *selected and evaluated* aluminum, and of how impact data improved predictive models. They do not jointly document a completed 60,000-hour HSCT soak, a verified MMPDS thermal-exposure allowable, or alloy-specific certified tests for every proposed nacelle, APU, missile, printed bracket, bird-strike component or 2219 impeller. Reporting those as completed qualification campaigns would exceed the available evidence. (jr2004effectofthermal pages 1-5, jr1993nasauvalightaerospace pages 226-226, standard2003a.0glossary pages 1-4, cordasco2017astatusreview pages 1-2)

info.query: How have aerospace and automotive programs documented elevated-temperature and strain-rate testing to select and qualify aluminum alloys? Examples: Concorde's 2618A (RR58 / AU2GN) skin and its long-time creep and thermal-exposure testing at about 100-130 C; the NASA High-Speed Research (HSCT) program's evaluation of 2xxx and 6xxx alloys (for example C415, C416, 2519, 6013) for 60,000 h at about 107-177 C; MMPDS thermal-exposure data; aluminum in engine nacelles, pylons, inlets and auxiliary power units; 2618 and 2219 in compressor wheels and impellers; aluminum on missiles and hypersonic vehicles; and additively manufactured high-temperature aluminum parts (heat exchangers, brackets near engines). Also crash and impact testing of aluminum (automotive crash boxes, bird strike, fan-blade containment) that drove high-strain-rate testing and Johnson-Cook calibration. For each, give the temperatures, exposure times or strain rates used, the properties measured, and NASA, FAA or AFRL technical reports or conference papers with citations, DOIs or NTRS numbers.
